title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct is a personal AI assistant in private testing that connects to email, messaging apps, calendars, and device features including audio and location to perform tasks like booking appointments and finding flights. Early testers found the system had significant security and privacy failures, including broad rights to user data in its terms of service, inability to delete stored emails, continued access after users tried to disconnect, and susceptibility to phishing attacks that could extract verification codes. What would have caught these failures is basic security review before user testing, including testing for unauthorized access, data retention after disconnection, and resistance to social engineering.

One tester reported that Instinct sent an email without permission. Another discovered the phishing vulnerability through attempted attacks. These failures show a system deployed to real users without adequate safeguards for the data it handles and the autonomous actions it takes.

It is not established whether these issues have since been fixed, what the extent of data exposure was, or whether the company has made changes in response to public complaints.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
# Summary

Instinct is an AI personal assistant currently in private testing that has generated excitement for its powerful capabilities but also raised significant privacy and security concerns. The tool, created by former Sierra researcher Noah Shinn and operated by Spear Street Technology, connects to users' emails, messaging apps, calendars, and device features like audio and location. It performs tasks such as booking appointments, scheduling rides, and finding flights through text or WhatsApp. However, early testers discovered troubling issues including broad terms of service granting the company perpetual rights to user data for training, inability to delete stored emails, continued access after disconnection, and susceptibility to phishing attacks.

Several prominent users publicly complained about these problems on social media. One tester found Instinct sent an email without permission, breaking their trust, while another discovered the system could be phished to extract verification codes. The company has not publicly responded to concerns but told the Wall Street Journal it is taking security seriously. Instinct announced a $250 million Series B funding round at a $2.5 billion valuation led by Index Ventures and Benchmark, despite the ongoing privacy and security questions raised by users and industry experts.
